Translation: "There is no better king for the realm of speech than me - It became certain for me to rule the kingdom of speech in the world."
Concept: This is about the poet claiming mastery over speech or poetry, asserting dominance in the realm of language. It's about self-praise and sovereignty in eloquence.

"بگماشت بالی تاج بر کشور خویش - تا در سر خویش کرد آخر سر خویش"
Translation: "He placed a feathered crown on his own country - Until at last he made his own head his own head."
This one is tricky. "بالی" might mean "wing" or "feather," and "تاج" is crown. So, "a feathered crown" could refer to something like a peacock feather crown. "در سر خویش کرد آخر سر خویش" – "made his own head his own head" seems redundant or metaphorical. Perhaps it's about someone adorning themselves or their domain, leading to self-realization or self-destruction. I recall this might be from a story, like in Attar's works, about a peacock. In Persian literature, this could be referring to the peacock who was proud of its feathers but ended up in a lower state. The phrase "در سر خویش کرد آخر سر خویش" might mean he brought about his own end or something similar. Concept: It could be about pride leading to downfall or self-deception.

"پس برآمد پوستش رنگین شده - که منم طاووس علیین شده"
Translation: "Then his skin emerged colorful - Saying, 'I am the peacock, become exalted.'"
"پوستش" might be "his skin" or "his appearance," and "رنگین شده" means became colorful. "طاووس" is peacock, and "علیین" might be a typo or variant; it could be "عالیین" meaning exalted or high. So, this is clearly about a peacock boasting about its beautiful feathers, claiming to be exalted. Concept: Pride in one's appearance or status, self-glorification.

"بر راستی بال نظر کرد و چنین گفت - امروز همه روی زمین زیر پر ماست"
Translation: "He looked at the truth with a wing and said thus - Today all the face of the earth is under our wing."

"بال" is wing, so "he looked with a wing at truth" doesn't make sense. Perhaps it's "he raised his wing and looked" or something. In context, this might be from Rumi or another poet about a bird, like an eagle or something claiming dominion. Concept: Asserting dominance or protection over the earth, similar to a bird of prey claiming territory.
